blocks.content: Cyclones and anticyclones are large-scale atmospheric circulation systems formed due to horizontal pressure differences. They are the most powerful weather-producing mechanisms in the troposphere and play a critical role in global heat redistribution. A cyclone is a low-pressure system with converging and rising air, whereas an anticyclone is a high-pressure system with diverging and descending air.
1. Cyclone – Concept and Dynamics

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: A cyclone is a low-pressure system with converging and rising air, while an anticyclone is a high-pressure system with diverging and descending air.
Tropical cyclone formation requires sea surface temperatures above 26.5°C up to 60m depth, high mid-tropospheric humidity, low wind shear, and at least 5° latitude for Coriolis force.
The structure of a tropical cyclone consists of a calm eye (10–50 km wide), a highly destructive eyewall, spiral rainbands, and upper-level outflow.
India experiences two peak cyclone seasons—Pre-monsoon (Apr–Jun) and Post-monsoon (Oct–Dec)—with the Bay of Bengal being more cyclone-prone.
Key advanced phenomena include the Fujiwhara Effect (two cyclones rotating around each other) and Rapid Intensification (wind speed increasing by 55 km/h in 24 hours).

blocks.content: • Formed around a center of low atmospheric pressure.
• Air converges at surface and rises vertically.
• Latent heat released during condensation strengthens the system.
• Rotation due to Coriolis force: Counterclockwise (NH), Clockwise (SH).
• Strong pressure gradient causes high wind speeds.
Forces Acting in a Cyclone
• Pressure Gradient Force – pulls air toward low pressure.
• Coriolis Force – deflects moving air.
• Centrifugal Force – balances inward pull in curved motion.
• Friction – slows wind near surface.
Balance of these forces creates gradient wind circulation.
2. Structure of a Tropical Cyclone
• Eye – 10–50 km wide calm center with lowest pressure.
• Eyewall – Most destructive zone with highest wind speed and intense rainfall.
• Spiral Rainbands – Bands of thunderstorms extending outward.
• Outflow – Diverging air at upper troposphere.
3. Life Cycle of Tropical Cyclone
• Formation (Tropical Disturbance).
• Intensification (Tropical Depression → Storm → Cyclone).
• Mature Stage (Well-developed eye).
A cyclone is a low-pressure system with converging and rising air, whereas an anticyclone is a high-pressure system with diverging and descending air.
• Weakening after landfall due to loss of moisture.
4. Conditions for Formation
• Sea surface temperature above 26.5°C up to depth of 60m.
• High humidity in mid-troposphere.
• Low vertical wind shear.
• Sufficient Coriolis force (minimum 5° latitude).
• Pre-existing low-pressure disturbance.
• Upper-level divergence.

7. Cyclones in India
• Bay of Bengal is more cyclone-prone due to higher sea surface temperature.
• Shallow continental shelf increases storm surge damage.
• Arabian Sea cyclones increasing in frequency.
• Two peak seasons: Pre-monsoon (Apr–Jun) and Post-monsoon (Oct–Dec).
• IMD classifies cyclones into Depression, Deep Depression, Cyclonic Storm, Severe Cyclonic Storm etc.
8. Naming Conventions
Hurricanes (Atlantic), Typhoons (Pacific), Cyclones (Indian Ocean). Names are assigned by WMO regional panels.
9. Anticyclones – Structure and Weather
• High-pressure center with descending air.
• Divergence at surface.
• Clockwise rotation in NH.
• Associated with clear skies and stable weather.
• Winter anticyclones can cause cold waves.

items: Coriolis force is essential for rotation: Cyclones rotate counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere.
Tropical cyclones require a minimum of 5° latitude to form because Coriolis force is insufficient near the equator.
The eyewall features the highest wind speeds and most intense rainfall, making it the most destructive zone, while the center (eye) remains calm.
Bay of Bengal is more cyclone-prone than the Arabian Sea due to higher sea surface temperatures and a shallow continental shelf.

11. Advanced Concepts for Competitive Exams
• Storm Surge – Abnormal rise of sea level due to cyclone winds and pressure drop.
• Fujiwhara Effect – Two cyclones rotate around each other.
• Rapid Intensification – Wind speed increases by 55 km/h in 24 hours.
• Occlusion – Occurs in temperate cyclones when cold front overtakes warm front.
• Climate change may increase intensity though not necessarily frequency.
MASTER EXAM POINTS

• Cyclones are low-pressure systems with converging winds.
• Tropical cyclones require warm ocean water.
• Eye is calm but eyewall is most destructive.
• Coriolis force is essential for rotation.
• Temperate cyclones form along fronts.
• Anticyclones bring stable weather.
